claims.text: Diffusion-mediated nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases from an initial non-equilibrium solid solution governs microstructural evolution in Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The rate and extent of intermetallic precipitation determine retention or loss of corrosion resistance.
The rate and extent of intermetallic precipitation determine retention or loss of high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Excessive intermetallic growth produces continuous, brittle grain-boundary networks.
Continuous intermetallic grain-boundary networks compromise corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy is a metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution with a homogeneous distribution of Mg and the other constituent elements.
The initial state contains minimal intermetallic phases.
Controlled isothermal annealing at 300–500 °C is the proposed intervention, with room-temperature samples serving as the comparison.
Annealing produces discrete Mg-containing intermetallic compounds.
The Mg-containing intermetallic compounds nucleate preferentially at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
At elevated temperature, Mg atoms segregate by diffusion and nucleate intermetallic phases.
The resulting Mg-rich intermetallic phases grow according to diffusion-limited kinetics.
Finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates may enhance corrosion resistance by acting as stable protective barriers.
Finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates may enhance oxidation resistance by acting as stable protective barriers.
Coalescence of intermetallic precipitates into continuous networks creates paths for rapid corrosion.
Coalescence of intermetallic precipitates into continuous networks degrades oxidation resistance.
A moderate amount of intermetallic precipitation will refine the microstructure relative to the as-cast metastable state.
Moderate intermetallic precipitation will maintain or improve passivation and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Excessive intermetallic formation will significantly reduce corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation protection.
The relevant service regime is 300–500 °C for durations permitting diffusion-driven transformation without full equilibration.
